desc:
On an n x n grid (0 empty, 1 blocked) lives a snake that covers exactly two adjacent cells. At the start it lies horizontally on (0,0) and (0,1). The goal is to have it lie horizontally on (n-1,n-2) and (n-1,n-1).

A move can be one of these (all cells that the snake would newly cover must be empty and inside the grid):

  • right: both cells shift one column to the right;
  • down: both cells shift one row down;
  • rotate clockwise: a horizontal snake on (r,c),(r,c+1) may become vertical on (r,c),(r+1,c) if (r+1,c) and (r+1,c+1) are empty;
  • rotate counter-clockwise: a vertical snake on (r,c),(r+1,c) may become horizontal on (r,c),(r,c+1) if (r,c+1) and (r+1,c+1) are empty.

The snake never moves left or up. Return the minimum number of moves to reach the goal, or -1 if it is impossible.

grid = [[0,0,0],
        [0,0,0],
        [0,0,0]]

result = 3      (down, down, right)
hints: The snake's position is described by one anchor cell and its orientation (horizontal or vertical). That is your node.
Number the states (r, c, orientation) with the anchor being the top-left cell of the snake. List, for a horizontal and for a vertical snake, which cells must be free for each of its moves.
Run BFS from (0, 0, horizontal) and stop when you reach (n-1, n-2, horizontal). Each state has at most 3 outgoing moves, so there are about 2n² states and 6n² edges.
editorial: Model the snake by the cell where its tail sits (the top-left one) and whether it is horizontal or vertical. A horizontal snake on (r,c) covers (r,c) and (r,c+1), a vertical one covers (r,c) and (r+1,c). That gives at most 2n² states, and every move costs one.

From a horizontal state (r,c,0): move right to (r,c+1,0) if (r,c+2) is free; move down to (r+1,c,0) if both cells below are free, and in that same situation also rotate to (r,c,1). From a vertical state (r,c,1): move down to (r+1,c,1) if (r+2,c) is free; move right to (r,c+1,1) if both cells to the right are free, and in that situation also rotate to (r,c,0).

BFS from the start state finds the shortest sequence. The target is the state (n-1,n-2,0). Time and memory are O(n²). Because the snake can only go right, down or rotate, the search is small, but a rotation is the only way to get through a one-cell-wide vertical passage, so ignoring it gives wrong answers.
